Surat al-Dhariyat

Al-Mahayimi said: It was named after it (al-Dhariyat) because it is the beginning of good things (al-khayrat), and so it resembles the divine care (al-'inayah al-ilahiyyah). It is a Meccan surah, and its verses number sixty.

Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim

The discussion on the interpretation of His, Exalted is He, saying:

[1] ﴿By those that scatter with a scattering﴾

﴿By those that scatter with a scattering﴾: it means the winds that scatter the vapours (al-bukharat) with a scattering, that is, a kind of scattering so that they gather them into clouds. Or it means the fertile women, for they scatter children (al-awlad), metaphorically likening the succession of children to what is blown away by the winds. Or it means the causes that scatter creation, among the angels and others; this is also a metaphor, in which things prepared to emerge from the hidden state of non-existence are likened to the winds that scatter grains and the like.

Al-Dhariyat is the active participle of (dhara), the defective (mu'tall) root, meaning he scattered and dispersed what he had lifted from its place. It is also said: adhra. As for (dhara'a), the hamzated (mahmuz) root, it means he brought into being and originated.

The Interpretation of His Words, exalted is He:

[2] ﴿So those that carry a load﴾

﴿So those that carry a load﴾ means: the clouds that carry the rains, which make the crops and trees grow, for the benefit of grains and fruits. As Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl said:

"I have submitted myself to Him to whom the clouds submit, carrying sweet, clear water."

Or it means the winds that carry the clouds, or the pregnant women, or the means of these things.

And (al-Wiqr) with a kasra on the waw, like (al-Himl) in weight and meaning. It was also read with a fatha on the waw, as a verbal noun that was used to name the thing carried.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 51, verse 3–4:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[3–4] ﴿By those that run with ease﴾ ﴿and those that distribute by command﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 4]

﴿By those that run with ease﴾: that is, the ships that run easily upon the sea, or the winds that blow in their directions, or the stars that move in their courses. And ﴿ease﴾ (yusran) is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (masdar), or [it means] a running that has ease.

﴿By those that distribute by command﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 4]: that is, the angels who distribute affairs, such as rains, provisions and other things, or whatever includes them and others of the causes of distribution, or the winds that distribute the rains by directing the winds.

Remarks:

The first: We have mentioned that these four matters may be four different things, and may be one matter with four aspects. The first is that transmitted from ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him: that the dhariyat (scatterers) are the winds, the hamilat (burden-bearers) are the clouds, the jariyat (runners) are the ships, and the muqassimat (distributors) are the angels. Some of them chose, regarding the "runners," that they are the stars, so that this would be an ascent from the lower to the higher: the winds are above that, the clouds are above the winds, the stars are above the clouds, and the angels are above all of them, descending with Allah's commands, both legislative and cosmic.

Al-Razi preferred that the closer view is that these are four attributes of the winds, and he elaborated on this at length.

The wording, in its essence, is broad enough to encompass all of this, and Allah knows best.

The second: The benefit of the particle (fa') — if it is said that they are attributes of the winds, it is to explain the order of matters in existence, for the scattering [winds] produce the clouds, which then distribute the rains over the regions. And if it is said that they are four matters, then the fa' indicates sequence in mention or in rank.

The third: Al-Razi mentioned several wisdoms in the oath:

One of them: The disbelievers at times acknowledged that the Prophet ﷺ was dominant in establishing proof, but they would attribute to him argumentation, and [claim] that he knew in himself the corruption of what he said, and that he overcame us through the strength of disputation rather than the truthfulness of speech. Just as some people, when their opponent establishes proof against them and leaves them no argument, say: "He overcame me because of his knowledge of the way of disputation and my inability in that." Yet he knows within himself that the truth is in his hand, so there remains for the demonstrating speaker no way but an oath, and he says: "By Allah, the matter is as I say, and I do not dispute with you falsely." This is because if he took another path, by mentioning another proof, then when that other proof is completed the opponent would say about it the same as he said about the first, that it is an affirmation of the strength of disputation knowledge, so nothing remains but silence, or clinging to faith and abandoning the establishing of proof.

The second: The Arabs used to guard against false oaths, believing that they leave dwellings desolate. Then the Prophet ﷺ "swore often by every noble thing," and that only increased him in elevation and steadfastness. They would thus come to know that he does not swear by them falsely, for otherwise the ill omen of oaths would have struck him, and he would have suffered harm at some times.

The third: The oaths by which Allah, exalted is He, swore are all proofs that He brought out in the form of oaths. An example of this is the saying of one who speaks to his benefactor: "By the right of your abundant blessings, I will never cease to thank you." He mentions the blessings, which are a beneficial cause for the continuance of thanks, and takes the path of an oath; likewise these things are all a proof of Allah's power over the restoration.

If it is said: Why did He bring them out in the manner of oaths? We say: Because when the speaker begins his speech with an oath, it informs the listener that he intends to speak a great word, so the listener attends to it more than if he knew the speech was not significant. So He began with the oath and incorporated the proof in the form of an oath, whereupon the listeners turned their attention to hearing it, and there came forth for them the clear demonstration and the firm exposition in the form of an oath. End.

**The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[5–6] ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is true﴾ ﴿and indeed the Judgment is surely to occur﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 6]

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is true﴾ is the answer to the oath (*jawab al-qasam*). The word *mā* here may be a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*) or a verbal-noun particle (*masdariyyah*). The promised thing is the establishment of the Hour and the resurrection of the dead from their graves. The word *ṣādiq* means *ṣidq* (truth): the noun is placed in the position of the verbal noun, or it belongs to the pattern of *ʿīshatin rāḍiyah* (a pleasing life), where the adjective takes the form of the active participle.

﴿And indeed the Judgment﴾ means the recompense for deeds: if they are good, the recompense is good, and if they are evil, the recompense is evil. ﴿is surely to occur﴾ means it will certainly take place. Qatadah said: that is the Day of Resurrection, the day when Allah requites His servants for their deeds.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 51, verses 7–9:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[7–9] ﴿By the sky having paths﴾ ﴿Indeed, you are in conflicting speech﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 8] ﴿Turned away from it is whoever is turned away﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 9]

﴿By the sky having paths﴾: that is, the various paths, which are the orbits along which the stars travel. The original meaning of (al-hubuk) (paths) is what appears like a track in sand and water when the wind strikes it; likewise, "hubk" of hair refers to the marks of its curling and crinkling. (Al-hubuk), with two dammas, is the plural of hibak, like mithal and mithl, or kitab and kutub, or of habika, like tariqa and turuq. Zuhayr said, describing a pond:

Crowned with the roots of the star-plants, a northern wind weaves it, and for the morning brightness of its water are the hubuk (ripples).

It is also said: "How beautiful is the hibak of this dove!" meaning the black line on its wing.

And from al-Hasan: "(Having paths)" means the stars. He said: they were given paths with good creation; they were given paths with the stars. This is because they adorn the sky, just as a patterned garment is adorned by its weaving, so the stars were likened to the lines of embroidery, metaphorically by way of metaphor (isti'arah).

And some of the scholars of astronomy (falak) said: al-hubuk is the plural of habika, in the sense of mahbuka, that is, bound together. So the meaning of "having paths" is having gatherings of stars bound to one another by cords of attraction (al-jadhibiyyah, gravitation), for every habika is a group of mutually attracting stars. The noble verse is therefore a text on the multiplicity of these gatherings and on the attraction which the Europeans claim to have discovered; and accordingly it is one of the scientific miracles of the Qur'an. End of quotation.

﴿Indeed, you are in conflicting speech﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 8]: that is, contradictory and mutually opposed. Ibn Zayd said: they speculate, saying: "This is sorcery," and they say: "This is only the fables of the ancients."

﴿Turned away﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 9]: that is, it is diverted from it. ﴿whoever is turned away﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 9]: that is, he is diverted away from the clear truth with complete diversion, for there is no diversion more severe than this.

Al-Qadi mentioned, regarding the relation between the thing sworn by and the thing sworn to, that it is the comparison of their statements in their divergence and the contrariness of their aims to the paths of the heavens in their distance from one another and the difference of their ends.

Then he indicated that they were not turned away by following proofs, but by adhering to conjecture and guesswork, through His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:

[10–13] ﴿Destroyed be the conjecturers,﴾ ﴿who are heedless in a flood of ignorance.﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 11] ﴿They ask, "When is the Day of Recompense?"﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 12] ﴿It is the Day when they will be tried over the Fire.﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 13]

(p-5525) ﴿Destroyed be the conjecturers﴾ means: cursed are those who rely on guesswork (takhmin), while abandoning the proofs of certainty.

﴿who are heedless in a flood of﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 11] means: in ignorance that engulfs them regarding the obligation to follow decisive proofs and to abandon feeble doubts. ﴿heedless﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 11] means: unmindful of what has come to them and what has been sent down to them, by immersing themselves in bodily pleasures and monopolizing hasty worldly portions.

﴿They ask, "When is the Day of Recompense?"﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 12] means: when is the Day of Requital, the Day on which God repays His servants for their deeds.

﴿It is the Day when they will be tried over the Fire.﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 13] means: they will be burned. The root of fitna (trial, testing) is the melting of a precious metal so that its adulteration becomes apparent; then the term was used for punishment, burning and the like.

Al-Qadi said: It is an answer to the question, i.e., it occurs on the day when they will be tried over the Fire, or it is "the day when they..." etc. The fatha on "yawma" is due to its being attached to a non-declinable (mabni) element, and what indicates this is that it has also been read in the nominative (raf').

[15–19] ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in gardens and springs﴾ ﴿taking what their Lord has given them. Indeed they were, before that, good-doers﴾ [51:16] ﴿They used to sleep but little of the night﴾ [51:17] ﴿and in the hours before dawn they would seek forgiveness﴾ [51:18] ﴿and in their wealth there was a right for the one who asks and the deprived﴾ [51:19]

﴿Indeed, the God-fearing﴾ means those who guarded themselves against God by obeying Him and avoiding His disobedience in this world, and by avoiding (p-5526) speculation, guesswork and conjecture in matters of belief, ﴿in gardens and springs﴾. ﴿Taking what their Lord has given them﴾ [51:16]. Ibn Jarir said: that is, carrying out what their Lord commanded them, fulfilling His obligations. Others said: that is, accepting what He gave them of the bliss of the Hereafter, being content with it.

This is the correct meaning. For this reason Ibn Kathir said: "What Ibn Jarir explained has a problem, because the saying of Him, Blessed and Exalted, ﴿taking﴾ [51:16] is a circumstantial clause (hal) attached to His saying ﴿in gardens and springs﴾. So the God-fearing are in the gardens and springs while ﴿taking what their Lord has given them﴾ [51:16], that is, of the bliss, joy and delight."

Then He pointed to the reason for their deserving this, by His saying:

﴿Indeed they were, before that﴾ [51:16], meaning: in this world, ﴿good-doers﴾ [51:16], that is, they had done their deeds well, because the love of God had overcome their hearts, its effects appearing in their actions and words, as He explained by His saying, Glorified is He:

﴿They used to sleep but little of the night﴾ [51:17], that is, they slept only a little, so that their souls would be strengthened to worship Him with vigour.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Anas concerning the verse that they used to pray between these two prayers, between Maghrib and 'Isha'. And from Muhammad ibn 'Ali: they did not sleep until they had prayed 'Atamah (the night prayer).

And from Mutarrif: Scarcely a night passed over them without them praying in it, at its beginning or its middle.

And from al-Hasan, who said: They did not sleep of the night except a little; they struggled through the night prayer.

Al-Ahnaf ibn Qays recited this verse and said: "I am not of the people of this verse."

And from al-Dahhak: the pause (waqf) is at His saying ﴿they used to sleep but little﴾ [51:17], meaning that the good-doers were few; then a new sentence begins: ﴿of the night they would sleep but little﴾ [51:17], where "ma" is a negation, meaning they did not sleep.

Ibn Kathir said: This view is far-fetched and forced.

(p-5527) A subtle point: In this noble sentence there are intensifications in describing these people as having little sleep and abandoning rest. This is expressed by the mention of "little" (qalil), by "the night", which is the time of sleep, by "hujua" (light sleep), which is slight sleep, and by the addition of "ma", because it indicates paucity.

In sum, the verse indicates the recommendation of night prayer and the blame of sleeping through the whole night. The hadiths on this are numerous and well known.

﴿And in the hours before dawn they would seek forgiveness﴾ [51:18]. Al-Qadi (al-Baydawi) said: that is, despite their little sleep and their much tahajjud (night prayer), when they reached the pre-dawn hours they began seeking forgiveness, as if they had committed sins during their night.

Al-Razi said: In the verse there is an indication that they used to perform tahajjud and strive, then they wished that their deed be greater than that and purer; so they sought forgiveness for their shortcoming. This is the way of the generous: he brings the fullest forms of generosity, considers it little, and apologises for his shortcoming; while the miser brings little and considers it much and boasts of it. There is also another, subtler, aspect: when He explained that they slept a little, and sleep is a requirement of nature, He said ﴿they would seek forgiveness﴾ [51:18], that is, for that amount of little sleep. There is another subtle point, which we explain in answer to a question: He praised them for little sleep and did not praise them for much staying awake, and did not say: "They used to stay awake much of the night." What is the wisdom in this, since staying awake is the hardship and the striving, not the sleeping? We say: as an indication that their sleep was an act of worship, since God praised them for being little sleepers, and that sleep led them to occupy themselves with another act of worship, namely seeking forgiveness, at the times before dawn, and it prevented them from self-admiration and arrogance.

Then he said: Seeking forgiveness may mean asking forgiveness by speech, by their saying: "Our Lord, forgive us." And it may mean asking forgiveness by action, that is, at the pre-dawn hours they perform another act seeking forgiveness, which is prayer. The first is more evident, and the second is more famous among the commentators. End of quotation. The second is supported by the reference to zakat in the verse after it, and zakat is often mentioned alongside prayer in many verses. The reason for expressing prayer by seeking forgiveness is to indicate that it (seeking forgiveness) is its important pillar in tahajjud and in other prayers as well, (p-5528) so it is a case of mentioning a part to mean the whole. Seeking forgiveness is mentioned in the prayer's remembrances in several places, such as in bowing, between the two prostrations, and at the end of the prayer, as recorded by the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and the authors of the Sunan. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to prolong the bowing, the prostration and the tahajjud for this reason.

Subtle point: Al-Zamakhshari said in Asas al-Balagha: The pre-dawn (al-sahar) was called "sahar" as a metaphor, because it is the time when the night turns back and the day approaches; it is the breathing-space of the dawn. End of quotation.

﴿And in their wealth there was a right for the one who asks and the deprived﴾ [51:19]. That is, the poor person who is modest (mutaʿaffif), who is thought to be rich and so is denied charity.

Qatada said: These are the two poor of the Muslims: the beggar who asks with his hand outstretched, and the modest poor man. For both of them there is a right upon you, son of Adam.

In the Sahih (of al-Bukhari and Muslim) it is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The needy man is not the one who is turned away by a morsel or two, or a date or two. Rather, the needy man is the one who finds no sufficiency to make him independent, and who is not noticed so that charity is given to him."

Imam Ahmad narrated from al-Husayn ibn 'Ali, may God be pleased with them both, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The one who asks has a right, even if he comes on a horse." Abu Dawud also narrated it, and traced it back (to a chain) from 'Ali, may God honour his face.

The "deprived" includes everyone who has no wealth, whoever has lost his wealth through a calamity, and whoever has been denied provision and is in need. However, the most important of its instances is the modest poor person; for this reason most of the scholars relied on this interpretation.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "In their wealth there is a right" beyond zakat, by which they join the ties of kinship, or by which they host a guest, or by which they carry the burdened.

(p-5529) Then Exalted is He pointed out that there is no need for speculation and conjecture in the domain of beliefs, because of the abundance of clear signs, by His saying, Glorified is He:

The discussion of His saying, Exalted is He:

[20] ﴿And in the earth are signs for those of certain faith.﴾

﴿And in the earth are signs for those of certain faith.﴾ That is: lessons and admonitions for the people of certainty (yaqin), namely those whom reflection leads to that in which the soul finds rest and the breast is relieved. They see therein, among what He has scattered (dhara'a) of the varieties of plants and animals, and of the expanses, mountains, deserts, rivers and seas, great lessons and signs, and witnesses speaking of the power of the Maker and His oneness, may His majesty be exalted.

The discussion on the interpretation of His, may He be exalted, saying:

[21] ﴿And within yourselves. Will you not then see?﴾

﴿And within yourselves. Will you not then see?﴾ That is: in their state of origin and their transition from one condition to another; the variety of their tongues and colours; what they have been created with of powers and volitions; the differences among them in intellect and understanding; what is in the structure of their limbs of wisdom in placing each limb in the location that needs it; and other things that no writer's pen can enumerate, nor any eloquent tongue.

The hadith scholar Ibn Abi al-Dunya recited in his book (*al-Tafakkur wal-I'tibar*, "Reflection and Contemplation") for his teacher Abu Ja'far al-Qurashi:

When you look, seeking a lesson, then look at yourself, for in you is a lesson.

You are the one who lives and wakes in the world, and all of its affairs are lessons.

You were turned about in childhood, then greatness took full possession of your person.

You are the one whose creation laments him: the hair and the skin lament him.

You are the one who is given and then stripped, and caution does not save him from being stripped.

You are the one who owns nothing of himself, and yet destiny is more entitled to what is his than he is.

(p-٥٥٣٠)

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[22] ﴿And in the sky is your provision, and what you are promised.﴾

﴿And in the sky is your provision, and what you are promised.﴾ By "the sky" (al-sama') is meant the clouds (al-muzn), and by "the provision" (al-rizq) is meant the rain, for it is the cause of sustenance (al-aqwat). By "what you are promised" (ma tu'adun) is meant the punishment from heaven, because the seizing of the earlier deniers came from that direction; and the address is to the polytheists of Makkah.

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[23] ﴿By the Lord of the heaven and the earth, indeed it is the truth, just as you are speaking.﴾

﴿By the Lord of the heaven and the earth﴾ — that is, the One who created them, so that they serve as evidence for the truth of what He has informed. ﴿Indeed it is the truth, just as you are speaking﴾ — that is, just as your speech is (true). The pronoun in (innahu) refers either to what was mentioned concerning the signs and provision, or to the matter of the Prophet ﷺ, or to what you are promised. The last view is supported by what follows of the reports of the threat against the deniers, beginning with the story of the people of Lot, because their settlements lie on the route they take to Palestine for trade. Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 51, verse 24–30:

They said, "Fear not," and gave him good tidings of a learned boy.﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 28] ﴿Then his wife approached in a loud cry and slapped her face and said, "[I am] an old, barren woman!"﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 29] (p-5531)﴿They said, "Thus said your Lord. Indeed, He is the Wise, the Knowing."﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 30]

Al-Zamakhshari said: In it is an exaltation of the story, and an alert that it is not from the knowledge of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but he knew it through revelation. And their honoring [lies in] that Abraham served them himself, had his wife serve them, and hastened to provide them hospitality; or [it means] that they themselves are honored.

﴿When they entered upon him and said, "Peace," he said, "Peace"﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 25], i.e., "Peace be upon you." ﴿[you are] a people unknown﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 25], i.e., you are a people whom I do not know. It is like a question from him about their condition, so that he may know them; for your saying to one whom you meet, "I do not know you!" is equivalent in force to your saying, "Make yourself known to me and describe yourself."

﴿So he turned quickly to his household﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 26], i.e., he went to them secretly away from his guests. It is among the etiquette of the host that he conceal his affair and hasten with the hospitality without the guest perceiving it, lest he (the guest) restrain him and excuse him. This is what al-Zamakhshari said, and al-Nasir supported it with what he related from Abu 'Ubayd: that it is not said "raagha" (to turn aside) except when one goes away in secrecy, and that it is said "rawwagha al-luqmah" (he dipped the morsel) when he soaks it so that it becomes saturated with ghee; al-Nasir said: "It is from this meaning, because it goes off dipped in the ghee until it is hidden." Among its inverted forms (maqlubat) is "ghawr al-ard" (the depression of the earth) and "al-jurh" (the wound), and the rest of its inverted forms are close to this meaning. End of quotation.

﴿So he brought a fattened calf﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 26], i.e., he had roasted it.

﴿And he presented it to them﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 27], i.e., by placing it before them. ﴿He said, "Will you not eat?"﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 27], i.e., of it. The judge (al-Qadi) said: It indicates that it was roasted in the hot ashes (hanidh). The hamza in it (a-la) is for offering and urging to eat, in the manner of courtesy, if he said it when he first set it down; and for denunciation (inkar), if he said it when he saw them turning away.

﴿And he sensed from them fear﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 28], i.e., he concealed it, supposing that they intended him harm. ﴿They said, "Fear not," and gave him good tidings of a learned boy﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 28], i.e., one who will reach maturity and perfect his knowledge.

﴿Then his wife approached in a loud cry﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 29], i.e., a shout; ﴿and slapped﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 29], i.e., struck; ﴿her face﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 29], i.e., in amazement, according to the custom of women regarding anything strange to them. (p-5532)﴿And said, "[I am] an old, barren woman!"﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 29], i.e., barren; I have no child.

﴿They said, "Thus said your Lord"﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 30], i.e., like what we have said and informed you of, your Lord has said it; for we only inform you about Allah, so accept His word, and do not imagine concerning Him a contradiction of wisdom, nor ignorance by your not accepting the bearing of a child. ﴿Indeed, He is the Wise, the Knowing.﴾

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 51, verses 38–40:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[38–40] ﴿And in Musa (Moses), when We sent him to Pharaoh with a clear authority.﴾ ﴿But he turned away with his pillar and said, "A magician or a madman."﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 39] ﴿So We seized him and his soldiers and cast them into the sea, and he was blameworthy.﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 40]

﴿And in Musa﴾ is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon "fīhā" (in it), with the preposition repeated, because the element conjoined upon is a pronoun in the genitive case. That is: and We left, in the story of Musa, with the destruction of his enemies, a sign and a proof that makes clear to whoever sees it the reality of his claim.

﴿When We sent him to Pharaoh with a clear authority﴾ means: with a manifest proof.

﴿But he turned away with his pillar﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 39] means: he turned away from faith. Al-rukn (the pillar, or side) is the side of a thing, so "ruknuhu" is the side of his body, and turning away with it is a metaphor (kinaya) for aversion. The bāʾ (with) here is for transitivity (taʿdiya), since its meaning is "he bent his side"; or it is for accompaniment/attendance (mulabasa); or al-rukn here means the army, since one leans upon it and is strengthened by it, and the bāʾ is for accompaniment or attendance.

﴿And said, "A magician"﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 39] means: he is a magician.

﴿Or a madman﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 39]. ﴿So We seized him and his soldiers and cast them into the sea﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 40] means: We drowned them in the sea. ﴿And he was blameworthy﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 40] means: he committed what deserves blame, namely disbelief and obstinacy.

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

Discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[49] ﴿And of everything We created pairs, that you may remember.﴾

﴿And of everything We created pairs﴾ That is: a male and a female, or two opposite kinds.

Ibn Kathir said: All created things are in pairs: heaven and earth, night and day, sun and moon, land and sea, light and darkness, faith and disbelief, life and death, wretchedness and happiness, Paradise and Fire. Even animals and plants. End of quote. This is taken from the words of Ibn Jarir in support of the tafsir of Mujahid. The wording of Ibn Jarir is: The more correct of the two opinions on this is the view of Mujahid, namely that Allah, blessed and exalted is He, created for everything He created a second, opposite to it in its meaning, so each of the two is a pair for the other. For this reason it was said: ﴿We created pairs﴾. Through His saying "His creation," may He be glorified and praised, He drew attention to His power to create whatever He wills, and that He is not like things whose nature is to produce only one kind and not its opposite. For everything whose attribute is to produce one kind only, such as fire, whose nature is to heat and which is not fit for cooling, and such as ice, whose nature is to cool and which is not fit for heating, it cannot be described as perfect. The perfection of praise belongs only to the One who is capable of doing whatever He wills among different and similar things. End of quote.

﴿that you may remember﴾ Ibn Jarir said: That is, so that you may take heed and reflect upon this, and thus you, O polytheists, may know that your Lord, who merits your worship, is the One who is able to create a thing and its opposite, and to originate pairs of everything, not one who is unable to do that.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 51, verse 50:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[50] ﴿So flee to Allah. Indeed, I am to you from Him a clear warner.﴾

﴿So flee to Allah﴾: that is, flee from His punishment to His mercy, by believing in Him, following His command, and acting in obedience to Him. Al-Shihab said: The command to flee from punishment is meant as a command to belief and obedience, because by obeying Him one is secure from punishment, as if one had fled to one's place of safety. Thus it is a metaphorical allegory (isti'arah tamthiliyyah).

﴿Indeed, I am to you from Him a clear warner﴾: that is, I warn you of His punishment and make you fear His torment, the torment with which He visited these nations whose stories He has related to you, and which He will make them taste in the Hereafter.

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[51] ﴿And do not set up with Allah another god. Indeed, I am to you from Him a clear warner.﴾

﴿And do not set up with Allah another god. Indeed, I am to you from Him a clear warner.﴾ That is: he has made the warning clear. Abu al-Su'ud said: In it is an emphasis on what precedes it, namely the command to flee from the punishment to Him, exalted is He; but not by way of repetition, as has been said, rather by forbidding its cause and making obligatory the fleeing from it.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 51, verses 52–54:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[52–53–54] ﴿Thus did there come no messenger to those before them but they said, "A sorcerer or a madman!" Have they bequeathed this saying to one another? Rather, they are a transgressing people.﴾ ﴿So turn away from them, and you are not to be blamed.﴾

﴿Thus﴾ means: just as they denied the Messenger and called him a sorcerer or a madman, as mentioned, ﴿so did there come no messenger to those before them but they said, "A sorcerer or a madman!"﴾ meaning by way of imitating their fathers and following their footsteps. Thus the source of their ignorance is one and the object of their obstinacy is one.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Have they bequeathed this saying to one another?﴾ is a rebuke and an expression of astonishment at their condition and their agreement upon that vile word, which hardly occurs to the mind of any sensible person, let alone utters it. That is: did some of them enjoin this saying upon others until they all agreed upon it?

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Rather, they are a transgressing people﴾ is a turning away from the idea that the basis of their agreement on evil is their mutual charge, and an affirmation that it is a matter more heinous than mutual charge, and more shameful than it, namely the transgression that encompasses all of them. This indicates that the utterance of that vile word by each one of them is, by the requirement of their wicked nature, and not by the compulsion of an injunction from those before them. This is what Abu al-Su'ud conveyed.

﴿So turn away from them﴾ means: turn away from confronting them with the worst, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and leave off their harm﴾ [al-Ahzab: 48], and His saying, ﴿and abandon them with a gracious abandonment﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 10]. ﴿And you are not to be blamed﴾ means: for their turning away, since you are not over them a tyrant nor a controller, and nothing of their reckoning is upon you.

Note:

The statement of some exegetes here, ﴿So turn away from them﴾, meaning: turn away from disputing with them after you have repeatedly called them to the message, is far removed from the meaning by a great distance; for disputing with them was something commanded continuously, since it is the greatest means of making the truth manifest, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and strive against them with it a great striving﴾ [al-Furqan: 52].

Likewise is the statement of some regarding His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And you are not to be blamed﴾, meaning: for your turning away after you have delivered the message, for it contradicts the command to remind them thereafter. The correct view is what we have mentioned in explaining the verse, for it is what is consistent with its counterparts. The most sound of the tafsirs is that which is by parallels and counterparts, as it has been said, and the best of what you explain is by what is transmitted.

The most sound of the tafsirs is that which is by parallels and counterparts, as it has been said, and the best of what you explain is by what is transmitted.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 51, verses 52–54:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[52–53–54] ﴿Thus did there come no messenger to those before them but they said, "A sorcerer or a madman!" Have they bequeathed this saying to one another? Rather, they are a transgressing people.﴾ ﴿So turn away from them, and you are not to be blamed.﴾

﴿Thus﴾ means: just as they denied the Messenger and called him a sorcerer or a madman, as mentioned, ﴿so did there come no messenger to those before them but they said, "A sorcerer or a madman!"﴾ meaning by way of imitating their fathers and following their footsteps. Thus the source of their ignorance is one and the object of their obstinacy is one.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Have they bequeathed this saying to one another?﴾ is a rebuke and an expression of astonishment at their condition and their agreement upon that vile word, which hardly occurs to the mind of any sensible person, let alone utters it. That is: did some of them enjoin this saying upon others until they all agreed upon it?

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Rather, they are a transgressing people﴾ is a turning away from the idea that the basis of their agreement on evil is their mutual charge, and an affirmation that it is a matter more heinous than mutual charge, and more shameful than it, namely the transgression that encompasses all of them. This indicates that the utterance of that vile word by each one of them is, by the requirement of their wicked nature, and not by the compulsion of an injunction from those before them. This is what Abu al-Su'ud conveyed.

﴿So turn away from them﴾ means: turn away from confronting them with the worst, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and leave off their harm﴾ [al-Ahzab: 48], and His saying, ﴿and abandon them with a gracious abandonment﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 10]. ﴿And you are not to be blamed﴾ means: for their turning away, since you are not over them a tyrant nor a controller, and nothing of their reckoning is upon you.

Note:

The statement of some exegetes here, ﴿So turn away from them﴾, meaning: turn away from disputing with them after you have repeatedly called them to the message, is far removed from the meaning by a great distance; for disputing with them was something commanded continuously, since it is the greatest means of making the truth manifest, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and strive against them with it a great striving﴾ [al-Furqan: 52].

The most sound of the tafsirs is that which is by parallels and counterparts, as it has been said, and the best of what you explain is by what is transmitted.

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[55] ﴿And remind, for indeed the reminder benefits the believers.﴾

﴿And remind﴾, i.e., admonish them. ﴿For indeed the reminder benefits the believers﴾, i.e., those whose faith God has decreed, or those who believe, for they are the ones intended from among creation, not others, since they are the worshippers.

The discourse on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[56] ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me.﴾

﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me.﴾ That is: for this wisdom, namely their worship of Him, exalted is He, by what He commanded through the tongue of His Messenger; for no righteousness is complete and no happiness in the two abodes is attained except through it. And His words, exalted is He:

The discussion on the interpretation of His, the Exalted's, saying:

[57–58] ﴿I do not want any provision from them, nor do I want them to feed Me.﴾ ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Provider, the Possessor of strength, the Firm.﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 58]

﴿Indeed, Allah is the Provider, the Possessor of strength, the Firm.﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 58] is an explanation of His greatness, mighty and majestic. His affair with His servants cannot be measured by the affair of created masters with their slaves. For their slaves are required to serve and to earn for their masters, and the masters' provisions are determined through the earnings of their slaves. Allah, the Exalted, does not demand provision or feeding from His servants. Rather, He is the One who provides for them, and He only demands of them that they worship Him, so that they may direct what He has bestowed upon them toward that for which they were created.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[59] ﴿Indeed, for those who wronged there is a portion like the portion of their companions, so let them not ask Me to hasten it.﴾

﴿Indeed, for those who wronged﴾ means those who wronged themselves by exposing themselves to the everlasting punishment through denying the Messenger, (p-5539) and through persisting in polytheism, transgression and corruption. ﴿A portion﴾ means an ample share of the punishment. ﴿Like the portion of their companions﴾ means like the shares of their counterparts among the nations that have been related. The origin of the word "dhanub" (bucket) is a large bucket full of water, or one nearly full. It may be masculine or feminine. It was borrowed to denote a share in general, whether evil, like the share of punishment in this verse, or good, as in the sense of a gift in the words of Amr ibn Shas:

And in every tribe you have bestowed a blessing, so a bucket is due to Shas from your generosity.

The word derives from water-carriers dividing water by buckets: one bucket is given to this one, and its like to another.

﴿So let them not ask Me to hasten it﴾ means: let them not demand of Me that I hasten it before its appointed time. It will surely reach them, but at its delayed time, for a wisdom.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 51, verse 60:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[60] ﴿So woe to those who disbelieve, from their day which they are promised.﴾

﴿So woe to those who disbelieve, from their day which they are promised.﴾ That is: they were warned that the descent of punishment upon them would occur on it, and what they would encounter in it of affliction and hardship. And "the day" (al-yawm) is either the Day of Resurrection or the Day of Badr.

Abu al-Su'ud said: The first is more fitting with the opening of the noble surah that follows.

The second is more in accord with what precedes it, in that both are part of the worldly punishment. And God knows best.
